issues.explanation: The bicycle trigger is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of relief work in a war zone unless there is some specific event history linking bicycles to the trauma. The other triggers (unwanted thoughts, heavy breathing sounds) fit much better with war-zone trauma, making the bicycle item stand out as clinically implausible in this profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance implies a persistent current sense of threat, but the formulation explicitly isolates Threat as inactive, with no active links to or from the other nodes. In this profile, memory and appraisal are tightly linked, but a strong 'I have to be on guard all the time' appraisal reads more like an active threat belief than a memory-based negative appraisal, so it does not align well with the formulation structure.

vignette:
Eleanor had spent months telling herself that the trip to the former war zone was over, that the work she had done there as a relief worker belonged to another life, but the memory never stayed where she put it. It would force its way into her mind at random moments, not as a full story but as pictures: a stretch of shattered street, a doorway half collapsed, a child's face in profile, the blur of dust hanging in sunlit air. She noticed that it felt strangely alien, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her, and that odd distance only made it more unsettling. When a siren cut through traffic outside city hall or a chair scraped sharply in the hearing room, that strange, unreal feeling made the war-zone images rush back with particular force, as if the sound had opened a door she had been trying to keep shut. After each intrusion, she found herself thinking that if a memory could feel so чужд and uncontrollable, then something in her must be damaged, and that thought made the images harder to dismiss the next time they surfaced. Since the deployment she had come to believe that if she thought about what she had seen she would not be able to handle it, and that belief made her flinch away from anything that might bring it back. Because she had come to see herself as unable to cope, she started registering the world differently, watching every hallway, doorway, and burst of noise for signs that something was about to happen. In city hall she found herself listening for heavy breathing on the stairs or a door slamming down the corridor, certain that any of it could mean the memory was about to break through again. That same conviction made the intrusive pictures more relentless: once she had decided she was not strong enough to bear them, the memory kept returning as proof of that weakness, vivid and insistent whenever she tried to put it out of mind. Yet the very effort to keep it down seemed to make it push harder against her mind, arriving uninvited when she was trying to prepare notes for council meetings or sit through an evening alone. Because the memory kept forcing its way back, she began to notice every cough in a hallway, every scrape of a chair, every abrupt footstep in city hall as if they might be the next signal that it was about to return, and those cues started to stand out against the ordinary noise of the day. The more often the images returned, the more those same sounds seemed to carry her straight back into the scene, so that a cough behind her or a sudden bang from a closing door no longer stayed in the present for long.

What frightened Eleanor most was how easily the world now seemed to press against that memory. Heavy breathing in a crowded corridor, the sharp bang of a door slamming in city hall, even a burst from a car backfiring outside her apartment could jolt her into a sudden state of alarm. Each of those sounds seemed to tell her, with an almost brutal logic, that nowhere was really safe and that danger could break in without warning, so ordinary spaces began to feel booby-trapped with reminders she could not ignore. In those moments the pictures returned at once, and the scene in her mind felt less like recollection than intrusion. A sound of heavy breathing on a busy committee floor could carry her straight back to the tense, waiting silence of the field clinic; a bang in the street could flood her with the same stark images of impact and wreckage. She found herself pulling away from stairwells, from loud meeting rooms, from places where she could not control the noise, because she had come to believe the world was a dangerous place and that danger could appear without warning. The more the memory leapt in, the more she watched the environment for signs of it, listening for breathing, scanning for sudden sounds, bracing before she even knew what had startled her.

That sense of danger fed back into the way Eleanor held the memory itself. She said it did not feel like her own life, only a set of vivid snapshots that had somehow attached themselves to her, and that detachment seemed to confirm her fear that something fundamental in her had been damaged. After a microphone cracked in the council chamber or a door banged in the corridor, the whole scene would surge back so quickly that she felt yanked straight into it again, and the sudden return of those images only deepened her sense that she was permanently altered and could not trust herself to cope. She worried that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again, because outside of the sharp fear and tightening dread there was little else she could reliably access. When she tried to think through what had happened, the images appeared first, and with them came the conviction that she had somehow crossed into a place from which ordinary feeling did not return. Then the thought of the event became another threat, something she avoided by burying herself in council work, staying late at meetings, and steering conversation away from anything that might touch on conflict or aid work. Even so, the pictures would still arrive, and when they did she would once again be looking for the sounds that set them off, as if preparing for the next blow.

Over time, the cycle narrowed her life. Eleanor kept attending her city council duties, but she sat closest to the door and grew tense whenever a microphone cracked, a folder slammed, or someone came in breathing hard from climbing the stairs. She began leaving receptions early, skipping crowded public forums, and arranging her days so she would not be caught in small enclosed rooms where a sudden bang might echo. Colleagues noticed that she seemed more distant, less patient, and she herself knew that the effort to stay ahead of the next trigger was exhausting. What had started as an attempt to avoid being overwhelmed by the memory had become a way of living inside constant alertness, because every sound seemed capable of summoning the same alien pictures and every picture seemed to prove that the danger was still near. By the time she finally sought help, it was not only the war-zone scenes that troubled her but the life she had built around not encountering them. She came in worried that if she kept avoiding the memory she would remain trapped in this narrowed, watchful version of herself, yet she was equally afraid that facing it directly would leave her unable to cope.

violations.explanation: No paragraph clearly states that triggers/reminders cause the memory to intrude; the vignette shows triggers occurring alongside intrusions, but not a direct trigger-to-memory causal link in the same paragraph.
No paragraph clearly shows triggers leading to negative appraisals; the sounds and cues evoke alarm and memories, but they are not described as causing the patient's negative beliefs or appraisals.
No paragraph clearly states that negative appraisals drive the intrusive memory; her beliefs about not coping are linked to avoidance, not to the memory intrusions themselves.
No paragraph clearly shows negative appraisals causing triggers/reminders to become salient or frequent; the beliefs lead to avoidance, but not to triggering cues.
No paragraph clearly states that the intrusive memory produces the negative appraisals; the memory is described as unsettling, but not as the cause of her beliefs about damage or inability to cope.
No paragraph clearly states that the memory produces the triggers/reminders; the cues are presented as external stimuli that summon the memory, not as something generated by the memory.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Memory: No paragraph clearly states that triggers/reminders cause the memory to intrude; the vignette shows triggers occurring alongside intrusions, but not a direct trigger-to-memory causal link in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph clearly shows triggers leading to negative appraisals; the sounds and cues evoke alarm and memories, but they are not described as causing the patient's negative beliefs or appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph clearly states that negative appraisals drive the intrusive memory; her beliefs about not coping are linked to avoidance, not to the memory intrusions themselves.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph clearly shows negative appraisals causing triggers/reminders to become salient or frequent; the beliefs lead to avoidance, but not to triggering cues.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph clearly states that the intrusive memory produces the negative appraisals; the memory is described as unsettling, but not as the cause of her beliefs about damage or inability to cope.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph clearly states that the memory produces the triggers/reminders; the cues are presented as external stimuli that summon the memory, not as something generated by the memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
